newsitem.title: INDIA: Scores of Calcutta's poor pray for Mother Teresa.
newsitem.headline: Scores of Calcutta's poor pray for Mother Teresa.

text.p: Many poor beneficiaries of Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity said on Thursday they were praying for the Roman Catholic nun as she battled a failing heart in a hospital in India's eastern city of Calcutta.
"Actually, I only read about her illness in a newspaper," said Madan Ghosh, who is staying in Prem Daan (Gift of Love), a home for the destitute run by Mother Teresa's religious order in Calcutta.
"But I am praying for her recovery," he added. "These sisters have helped me a lot."
Mother Teresa was gaining strength after undergoing surgery to clear two blocked arteries last week, her doctors said.
"She is looking fresh but she is still not out of danger," they said in a medical bulletin early on Thursday.
The effects of old age and a life of hard work in Calcutta's slums have left Mother Teresa, 86, with kidney troubles and weak lungs, which doctors say are slowly responding to medication.
Ghosh said he came to Calcutta in search of a job a few months ago from his home town of Guwahati, the capital of the nearby northeastern state of Assam.
"I fell ill, with violent, twisting pains in my stomach," he said. "Then somebody brought me here."
Prem Dan is one of five homes Mother Teresa's order runs in Calcutta to comfort and console misfits, outcasts and others too broken or wearied by life's problems to carry on alone.
Ghosh was one of more than 100 men sitting on the floor around a large open dining hall, each using his fingers to scoop up a meal of rice, meat and potatoes from an aluminium dish.

Two nuns wearing the white saree edged with three blue stripes that identifies Mother Teresa's order stood behind a table at one end of the room, ladling the food on to plates held by volunteer workers.
In a nearby dormitory, half a dozen men lay dozing or inert on steel-framed cots with plain cotton-covered mattresses.

A nun on duty pointed to one with a bandaged right leg. "When he came in yesterday, we removed so many worms from his wound," she said, cupping her hands to demonstrate. "You would not have believed it. You need a special grace from God to do this work."

In the women's section sat Protima, who said she came to Prem Dan three months ago, suffering from tuberculosis. With a woollen blanket around her shoulders, and the scabs of the first stage of chicken-pox marking her face, she spoke reluctantly.
"We are worried about Mother Teresa," she said. "I used to see her quite often. She is a good person."

At Nirmal Hriday (Innocent Heart), another of Mother Teresa's homes for the poor, a prayer hung on the wall. "Give me singleness of purpose," it said. "Give me the strength to lift at least a part of the burden of my suffering fellow men."
Nearby, Sister Dolores struggled to persuade Basu , with a large shaven head and sad eyes, to take a bath.
"On the streets, they're not used to bathing every day," the nun said, as Basu grunted and gesticulated angrily. "This cold weather makes them more reluctant. But we insist."

At the Mother House, the order's headquarters, the day begins with the nuns gathering to pray in a simple first-floor chapel. They sit on rough brown carpets. On the wall beside the crucifix is written, "I thirst".
At the left of the entrance, a wooden nameplate says "Mother Teresa, M.C." A tiny sliding shutter beside the white-painted name has been slipped aside so that the visitor can read, "Out".
